newsitem.title: INDIA: Suspected spot found on Mother Teresa's brain.
newsitem.headline: Suspected spot found on Mother Teresa's brain.

text.p: A suspected spot has been detected on Mother Teresa's brain after the 86-year-old Roman Catholic missionary fell while getting out of bed and hit her head, a doctor said on Tuesday.

"We have detected a suspected spot in the initial scan report and we are awaiting a detailed report," Dr A.K. Bardhan of Woodlands Nursing Home in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta told Reuters. He said the revered nun was in a stable condition.

Mother Teresa was admitted to the hospital's intensive care unit on Monday after she suffered an injury above her right eye in the fall. After she was admitted to the hospital, doctors said her condition was not serious.

Mother Teresa, known as the Saint of the Gutters for her devotion to the poor and destitute, was admitted to the same hospital on August 20 with heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia. She was released 18 days later and told to rest in bed.

"Her condition is stable, but we are going to observe her for some more days," said Bardhan, the hospital's leading heart expert. He said Mother Teresa did not want to remain in hospital, "but this time we are not releasing her immediately."
Bardhan said the hospital had asked a senior neurologist to examine Mother Teresa later on Tuesday. A medical report based on a more thorough study of the brain scan was expected later in the day.
On Monday, doctors said Mother Teresa continued to have an irregular heart beat, which she has suffered since her stay in the hospital in late August and early September.
Mother Teresa, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979, was fitted with a cardiac pacemaker in 1989.
In 1991, she was treated at a Californian hospital for heart disease and bacterial pneumonia. Two years later she fell in Rome and broke three ribs.
In August 1993, she developed malaria, complicated by heart and lung problems. Last April she fractured her left collar bone.
The Missionaries of Charity, which she founded in 1949, runs some 544 homes for unwanted children and the destitute in more than 80 cities.
The work includes caring for nearly 7,000 children in 120 homes and arranging 1,500 adoptions each year.
